items.stem: Which average is the value that occurs most often?
items.answer: The mode
items.markingKey: Mode = most frequent value.

items.stem: Explain why the median is often a better average than the mean for house prices in a city.
items.answer: A few very expensive houses (extreme values) raise the mean a lot, while the median, the middle value, is not affected by them, so it better represents a typical price.
items.markingKey: B1 extreme values/outliers affect the mean; B1 median unaffected so more typical [2]

items.stem: Explain why the mode is the most useful average for a shop deciding which shoe sizes to stock.
items.answer: The shop needs to know which size sells most often; the mean or median could be a size that is not the most popular, or not even an actual shoe size.
items.markingKey: B1 most common size; B1 mean may not be an actual size [2]

items.stem: The times, in minutes, that 8 students took to travel to school are: 18, 8, 42, 12, 31, 25, 25, 29. Find (a) the mode (b) the median (c) the range (d) the mean.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 25 (b) M1 orders the data; A1 25 (c) B1 34 (d) M1 190 ÷ 8; A1 23.8 [6]

items.stem: The mean of the 6 numbers 12, 14, 21, 16, 12 and x is 17. Find the value of x.
The heights, in centimetres, of 10 tomato plants are: 55, 52, 64, 64, 49, 41, 71, 56, 57, 30. (a) Find the mode. (b) Find the median. (c) Find the range.
What is the range of 3, 9, 4, 12, 7?
Explain why the mean of a data set can be a value that does not appear in the data.
items.answer: The mean is the total shared equally between the values, so it can be a value in between, or a decimal, even if no item has that value.
items.markingKey: B1 total ÷ number; B1 need not be a data value [2]

items.stem: Freya says the mode of 8, 5, 3, 7, 10, 12, 2, 1, 7 is 2 because the most common value appears 2 times. Explain the mistake.
items.answer: The mode is the value that occurs most often, 7, not the number of times it occurs (2).
items.markingKey: B1 mode is the value not the frequency; B1 mode = 7 [2]

items.stem: Elena is asked for the median of 13, 18, 7, 12, 15, 37, 9 and answers 12, the middle number in the list. Explain the mistake and find the correct median.
items.answer: The data must be put in order first: 7, 9, 12, 13, 15, 18, 37, so the median is 13.
items.markingKey: B1 must order the data; B1 median 13 [2]

items.stem: The midday temperatures, in °C, in Riyadh from Monday to Sunday were: −11, −8, −10, −9, −7, −6, −3. Find the range and the median temperature.
items.answer: Range 8 °C; median −8 °C
items.markingKey: M1 −3 − (−11); A1 range 8; B1 median −8 [3]

items.stem: The midday temperatures, in °C, in Mumbai from Monday to Sunday were: 3, 0, −1, 4, 3, −4, −7. Calculate the mean temperature, correct to 1 decimal place, and find the range.
items.answer: Mean −0.3 °C; range 11 °C
items.markingKey: M1 total −2 ÷ 7; A1 −0.3; B1 range 11 [3]

items.stem: The number of emails Amara received on each of 10 days are: 17, 7, 23, 6, 11, 23, 22, 18, 24, 5. (a) Find the mode. (b) One more value is added and the mean of all 11 values becomes 17. Find the value that was added.

In a grouped frequency table, which value is used to represent each class when estimating the mean?
items.answer: The midpoint of the class
items.markingKey: The exact values are unknown, so the midpoint is used.

items.stem: Explain why the mean calculated from a grouped frequency table is only an estimate.
items.answer: The actual data values are not known; each value is assumed to be at the midpoint of its class.
items.markingKey: B1 original values unknown; B1 midpoints used [2]

items.stem: Explain why you cannot find the exact range from a grouped frequency table.
items.answer: Only the class limits are known, not the actual smallest and largest values.
items.markingKey: B1 actual values unknown; B1 only class boundaries [2]

items.answer: Median 4; mean 4.04

items.answer: (a) 20 < h ≤ 25 (b) 15 < h ≤ 20 (c) The exact values are not known; each value is assumed to be at the midpoint of its class.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 20 < h ≤ 25 [1] (b) M1 position (58 + 1) ÷ 2 = 29.5; A1 15 < h ≤ 20 [2] (c) B1 midpoints / exact values unknown [1]

items.stem: The modal class of a grouped frequency table is
options: the class with the largest values
the class with the highest frequency
items.answer: the class with the highest frequency
items.markingKey: Modal = most frequent.

items.stem: The table shows the times spent on homework by students. Time (t minutes): 0 < t ≤ 10, 10 < t ≤ 20, 20 < t ≤ 30, 30 < t ≤ 40, 40 < t ≤ 50; Frequency: 2, 2, 14, 5, 8. Aisha estimates the mean using the upper end of each class and gets 34.8 minutes. Explain why this is not a good estimate and find a better one.
items.answer: Using upper ends assumes every value is as large as possible, so it overestimates. Using midpoints gives 29.8 minutes.
items.markingKey: B1 should use midpoints / overestimates; B1 29.8 [2]

items.stem: The table shows information about 17 customers. Shoe size: 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41; Frequency: 1, 2, 5, 7, 1, 1. Lina says the mean is 231 ÷ 6 = 38.5. Explain the mistake and find the correct mean.
items.answer: Lina found the mean of the values listed, ignoring how often each occurs. Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf = 654 ÷ 17 = 38.5.
items.markingKey: B1 frequencies must be used; B1 38.5 [2]

items.stem: The table shows information about 34 students. Number of brothers and sisters: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Frequency: 1, 2, 8, 12, 11. Tomás calculates the mean as 98 ÷ 5 = 19.6. Explain the mistake and find the correct mean.
items.answer: Tomás divided by the number of columns (5) instead of the total frequency (34). Mean = 98 ÷ 34 = 2.88.
items.markingKey: B1 divide by total frequency 34; B1 2.88 [2]

items.stem: The interquartile range is
options: the largest value minus the smallest value
the upper quartile minus the lower quartile
the median minus the lower quartile
items.answer: the upper quartile minus the lower quartile
items.markingKey: IQR = UQ − LQ.

items.stem: Explain why the interquartile range is less affected by an outlier than the range.
items.answer: The IQR uses only the middle half of the data, between the quartiles, so a single extreme value at either end does not change it much, whereas the range uses the extreme values directly.
items.markingKey: B1 IQR uses middle 50%; B1 range uses largest and smallest [2]

items.stem: Explain what a small interquartile range tells you about a set of data.
items.answer: The middle half of the data are close together, so the data are consistent / not very spread out.
items.markingKey: B1 middle 50% close together; B1 consistent / little spread [2]

items.stem: The times, in minutes, that 11 students took to travel to school are: 11, 38, 26, 40, 18, 36, 32, 27, 42, 6, 34. Find the interquartile range.
items.answer: 20 minutes

items.stem: Lucas is finding the interquartile range of 15, 21, 31, 6, 36, 49, 28, 43, 3, 4, 19. Lucas takes the 3rd and 9th numbers in the list, 31 and 3, and writes IQR = 28. Explain the mistake and find the correct IQR.
items.answer: The data must be put in order first: 3, 4, 6, 15, 19, 21, 28, 31, 36, 43, 49. LQ = 6, UQ = 36, so IQR = 30.

items.stem: For the data 5, 7, 10, 15, 17, 20, 21, 27, 30, 31, 33, Tariq says the interquartile range is 33 − 5 = 28. Explain the mistake and find the correct interquartile range.
items.answer: 28 is the range (largest − smallest). IQR = UQ − LQ = 30 − 10 = 20.

To compare two distributions fully, you should compare
options: an average and a measure of spread
items.answer: an average and a measure of spread
items.markingKey: One comparison of typical value and one of consistency.

items.stem: Explain why comparing only the means of two data sets may not be enough.
items.answer: Two sets can have the same mean but very different spreads, so you also need a measure of spread (range or IQR) to compare how consistent they are.
items.markingKey: B1 same average can hide different spread; B1 need a measure of spread [2]

items.stem: Explain what it means in context if the journey times on one bus route have a smaller interquartile range than another.
items.answer: The journey times on that route vary less, so they are more reliable/predictable.
items.markingKey: B1 times vary less; B1 more reliable in context [2]

items.stem: The journey times for two bus routes are: Route 1: 39, 40, 56, 68, 67, 46, 69; Route 2: 46, 49, 55, 47, 53, 48, 45. Calculate the mean and range for each, and make two comparisons.
items.answer: Route 1: mean 55, range 30; Route 2: mean 49, range 10. Route 1 has a higher mean (55 compared with 49), so on average Route 1's values are higher. Route 2 has a smaller range (10 compared with 30), so Route 2's values are more consistent.
